Series::conj¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::conj() const

What It Does¶

Returns the complex conjugate of each element: real - imag * i.

For a complex input the dtype is preserved (Complex64 -> Complex64, Complex128 -> Complex128) and only the sign of the imaginary part flips. For a real input conj() is the identity and returns a copy, so it is safe in dtype-agnostic code.

Conjugation is the operation behind a Hermitian transpose, the modulus (z * conj(z) = |z|^2), and the inner product on a complex vector space.

Reflection Across The Real Axis¶

Writing a value as z = x + yi makes the operation concrete:

conj(z) = x - yi

The real coordinate and magnitude stay fixed; only the direction is reflected. Consequently angle(conj(z)) is -angle(z) away from the branch cut, and two applications restore the original value. Conjugation is elementwise. It does not transpose a matrix; use adjoint() when both conjugation and swapping the final two dimensions are required.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series The conjugate, same shape and same dtype as the input. A real input yields an unchanged copy.

Gradient¶

conj() is differentiable. Its backward is itself: a cotangent g flowing back through z.conj() accumulates conj(g) into z. This holds on every backend and for both Complex64 and Complex128; on a real input it is the plain identity.

Examples¶

Example 1. Conjugating a complex series flips the imaginary sign.

auto z = pluss::make_series(
    {std::complex<float>{3, 4}, {-1, 0}, {0, 2}, {0, 0}});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.conj()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=complex64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[(3.0000-4.0000j), (-1.0000-0.0000j), (0.0000-2.0000j), (0.0000-0.0000j)]

Example 2. On a real input conj() returns the values unchanged.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-3.0, 0.0, 2.5}).conj()
) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-3.0000, 0.0000, 2.5000]

Example 3. Conjugation is its own inverse: conj(conj(z)) == z. This time the series is built from separate real and imaginary parts with pluss::series::complex.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(
    pluss::make_series({3.0f, -1.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f}),
    pluss::make_series({4.0f,  0.0f, 2.0f, 0.0f}));

pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.conj().conj()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=complex64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[(3.0000+4.0000j), (-1.0000+0.0000j), (0.0000+2.0000j), (0.0000+0.0000j)]

Example 4. Multiplying by the conjugate removes phase and leaves squared magnitude. The two independently written expressions agree elementwise.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(
    pluss::make_series({{3.0f, -1.0f}, {0.0f, 0.0f}}),
    pluss::make_series({{4.0f,  0.0f}, {2.0f, 0.0f}}));
pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.mul(z.conj()).real()) << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.abs().square()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 25.0000 1.0000 ⎤
⎣  4.0000 0.0000 ⎦
Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 25.0000 1.0000 ⎤
⎣  4.0000 0.0000 ⎦

This identity is often preferable to manually squaring and adding the two components because it states the complex-number intent directly.

Example 5. Reverse propagation is conjugated too. The imaginary component of conj(z) is -imag(z), so summing that component contributes 0 - 1j to every source element.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(
    pluss::make_series({{3.0f, -1.0f}, {0.0f, 0.0f}}),
    pluss::make_series({{4.0f,  0.0f}, {2.0f, 0.0f}}));
z.tracks_slope_(true);
z.conj().imag().sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.sensitivity()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=complex64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ (0.0000-1.0000j) (0.0000-1.0000j) ⎤
⎣ (0.0000-1.0000j) (0.0000-1.0000j) ⎦

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • conj() keeps the complex dtype; it does not return real parts. Use real() for that.

  • conj() is elementwise and leaves matrix dimensions in place. It is not a Hermitian transpose by itself.

  • On a real input it is a copy, not a view.

  • The result is materialized as an ordinary series. Mutating it does not alter the source.

Summary¶

conj() is the complex conjugate real - imag * i:

  • dtype-preserving on complex, identity on real

  • self-inverse: conj(conj(z)) == z

  • differentiable on every backend, with backward conj(g)

See Also¶

  • Series::real / Series::imag: the components; conj negates the second.

  • Series::abs: |z| = sqrt((z * conj(z)).real()).

  • Series::angle: conj negates the phase.

  • Series::adjoint: conjugate and transpose the final two dimensions as one matrix operation.

  • pluss::series::complex: build a complex series from real and imaginary parts (or pass std::complex values straight to pluss::make_series).
